**Where we are ahead:** the only Zig webhook-signature module found; constant-time compare, key
rotation (any active secret verifies), a `router` middleware that reads the raw body before any
parsing, allocation-free, and GitHub's own published vector as an external anchor.
**Where we are behind** (re-checked 2026-10-04): no replay *cache* (a `webhook-id` seen twice
inside the window is the caller's to refuse — svix does not keep one either), no typed event
payloads (octokit), no sender-side HTTP delivery/retry (svix's server). Built since the survey:
Standard Webhooks `v1` + `v1a`, Stripe, Slack, the replay-tolerance window on all three, base64,
SHA-1/SHA-512, and the middleware for every scheme.

Design + threat notes for auditors. Usage: see ./README.md. Attribution/provenance: see /NOTICE.

## Design & invariants
Constant-time compare of the computed vs received signature (`std.crypto.timing_safe.eql`) — never a
byte-wise early-exit compare. Key rotation: verification accepts any of a set of active secrets
(rotate without downtime); signing uses the primary. HMAC via `std.crypto.auth.hmac` (SHA-256);
allocation-free; the signature is always **lowercase hex** — no base64 variant is implemented. The
header name and the value prefix in front of the hex are both configurable, which covers GitHub's
own scheme (`X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hex>`) exactly. The middleware reads the
raw body **before** any parsing so the MAC covers exactly the bytes received. Immutable after init
(secret set + config fixed); no shared mutable state, so sharing a single `Verifier` across all
connection threads is safe without locking. Clean-room from RFC 2104 (HMAC) and the publicly-
documented GitHub `X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hex>` webhook convention — see NOTICE.

**Schemes (2026-10-04).** All MACs go through one helper (`macParts`: HMAC over the
concatenation of parts, so `id.ts.body` is never assembled in memory) and one constant-time
compare (`macEql`: `timing_safe.eql` over a zero-padded 64-byte array, so SHA-1/256/512 compare as
one fixed size); a presented MAC is decoded only at its digest's exact encoded length (a
truncated value whose missing bytes are zero would otherwise compare equal).
- **Standard Webhooks** (`standard`): signed content `id.ts.body`, the timestamp re-spelled as
  plain decimal (as the reference libraries format the parsed value); `webhook-signature` is a
  space-separated list, `v1,<b64>` checked against every secret and `v1a,<b64>` against every
  public key, unknown versions skipped. `whsec_` (prefix optional, base64 padded or not) must
  decode to the spec's 24–64 bytes; `whpk_` to 32; `whsk_` to the 32-byte seed or the 64-byte
  seed‖public layout (the spec does not fix it; the public half must match). `signEd25519` is
  RFC 8032 deterministic, so it needs a scratch buffer (std's streaming signer is randomized).
- **Stripe** (`stripe`): the first `t=` wins; every `v1=` is tried; `v0=` and others ignored;
  the `whsec_…` endpoint secret is the HMAC key as text (Stripe does not base64-decode it).
- **Slack** (`slack`): `v0=<hex>` over `v0:ts:body`.
- **Timestamps** (`checkTimestamp`): 1–19 ASCII digits, nothing else; refused when more than
  `tolerance_s` from `now` either way (inclusive boundary, as the reference's `now - ts >
  tolerance`); arithmetic in i128, so `now` at the i64 extremes cannot overflow. Stripe's SDKs
  check only the past; a timestamp from the future is refused here too.
- **Bounds:** `max_signatures` = 16 entries per header (more is `InvalidHeader`), of them
  `max_ed25519_signatures` = 4 `v1a` (each Ed25519 check re-hashes the body, so this × the key
  count bounds the body passes); `max_keys` = 8 per verification (free functions ignore extras,
  `Verifier.init` asserts). Each HMAC is computed once per key, not per presented signature.
- **Middleware:** `Options.scheme` picks the headers; for timestamped schemes `checkFreshness`
  runs on the headers alone and a stale delivery gets 401 before the body is read (so a stale
  oversized body is 401, not 413). A `Clock` is required (asserted); with asserts compiled out a
  missing clock reads `now = 0`, which refuses everything (fail closed).

## Threat model / out of scope
Defends against forged/unauthenticated webhook calls (an attacker without the secret cannot produce a
valid MAC) and against timing side-channels on the compare. **Replay:** a captured valid request can
be replayed for as long as its timestamp stays inside `tolerance_s` (the timestamped schemes); the
GitHub-style prefixed scheme carries no timestamp at all, so freshness there is the caller's. A
replay inside the window needs a seen-id cache, which is the caller's (the module keeps no state).
Ed25519 `v1a` verification is std's (strict, cofactorless); a non-canonical signature or key is
simply no match. Out of scope: secret storage/distribution, transport security (TLS is the
server's). Secret material lives in caller memory and in the `Verifier`'s copies; the module does
not zeroize it.

## Verification
An HMAC-SHA256 known-answer check, sign→verify round-trip and GitHub-style
(`sha256=<hex>`) header-format parse/reject tests, constant-time-compare accept/reject, key-rotation
(old+new secret) acceptance, tamper negatives (wrong secret, mutated body → reject). There is no
Stripe-format test — no Stripe parsing exists to test (see above). Run: `zig build test-webhooksig`.

**2026-10-04 (mvp → core).** Expected values from outside the module: the Standard Webhooks
reference libraries' own sign test (`libraries/go/webhook_test.go` `TestWebhookSign`:
`whsec_MfKQ9r8GKYqrTwjUPD8ILPZIo2LaLaSw`, `msg_p5jXN8AQM9LWM0D4loKWxJek`, 1614265330 →
`v1,g0hM9SsE…`) and its multi-signature list; Slack's documented worked example (docs.slack.dev,
re-verified with Python `hmac`); for the schemes no provider publishes a vector for, Python's
`hmac` (Stripe, SHA-1, SHA-512, base64) and `openssl pkeyutl -sign` over RFC 8032 TEST 1's key
(`v1a`), all as black boxes. The tolerance boundary is tested at exactly ±300 s (passes) and
±301 s (refused); every scheme goes through the middleware over the wire. **Seeded sweep**
(deterministic, ~0.3 s): 6 000 hostile header sets built from scheme fragments and damaged go
through `standard`/`stripe`/`slack.verify` and three `Format`s — an accepted header must contain
the one genuine signature in the fragment list, nothing else is ever accepted; reach pinned
(measured: 5 genuine, 92 too old, 187 too new, 6 174 bad timestamps, 2 379 bad headers, 9 163
no-match). Its oracle half signs random keys/ids/timestamps/payloads under all three timestamped
schemes, verifies, and requires one flipped byte of signature, id or payload to be refused
(4 500 round trips, 5 940 flips refused). **Mutation 2026-10-04:** 37 mutants (schemata,
ReleaseSafe), 3 survived the first run, each killed by a test added with its reason (a signature
one byte short whose missing byte is zero; secret/key sizes outside the spec; unpadded base64);
0 surviving. **CT gate:** `check-ct-compare` counts 1 `timing_safe.eql` site (was 2: both now go
through `macEql`) and 4 plain `std.mem.eql` (was 2: the new two compare the public version tags
`v1`/`v1a`) — the pin in `scripts/checks/ct-compare-expected.tsv` needs `1	4`.

**External anchor, and one refuted.** RFC 4231 (HMAC-SHA-2 test vectors) was evaluated and
deliberately **not** adopted: this module's `Hmac` is `std.crypto.auth.hmac.sha2.HmacSha256` used
directly, so RFC 4231 anchors a primitive already covered by Zig std's own test suite, not this
module's contribution — adding it would test std.crypto through a pass-through, not this code. The
module's actual contribution — the `sha256=<hex>` framing (`computeHex`'s hex formatting,
`sign`/`verify`'s prefix handling) — has a real anchor instead: GitHub's own webhook-validation docs
publish a canonical secret/payload/signature triple (`secret = "It's a Secret to Everybody"`,
`body = "Hello, World!"`, `sha256=757107ea0eb2...`) explicitly so third-party implementations can
self-check against it; independently re-verified here with `openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac` before
adoption. Recorded as a provenance note in this module's README `Provenance:` statement (a short factual test-oracle
triple, not a vendored corpus — no dedicated `modules/webhooksig/NOTICE` file).

## Backlog / deferred
**2026-10-04:** all three survey items are **done** (Standard Webhooks v1/v1a, Stripe, Slack with
a tolerance window; base64; SHA-1/SHA-512; Ed25519). Still deferred: a seen-id replay cache inside
the window (needs state and a clock the module does not own; a caller's `ramcache`/`kv` keyed by
`webhook-id` for `tolerance_s` does it), other providers' bespoke shapes (Twilio's URL+params
signature, AWS SNS certificates) until a consumer asks.

**Survey 2026-09-30** (checked with `rg -n -i 'tolerance|timestamp|max_age' src/root.zig`: only the "not implemented" comment at root.zig:7):
- **(survey 2026-09-30) Timestamped schemes with a replay tolerance** — Stripe (`t=…,v1=…`, MAC over `timestamp.body`), Slack (`v0:timestamp:body`) and Standard Webhooks (`id.timestamp.body`, base64) are the schemes most webhook receivers meet, and all carry a freshness window that this module cannot express; the SPEC already names Stripe. Effort: small–medium per scheme (a signed-payload builder, a header parser, a caller-supplied `now`, tolerance check; no clock in the module, per the house rule). Fits §2: yes.
- **(survey 2026-09-30) Base64 signature encoding and other digests (SHA-1, SHA-512)** — hex/SHA-256 only today; some providers use base64 or SHA-1. Effort: small. Fits §2: yes.
- **(survey 2026-09-30) Ed25519 asymmetric verification** (Standard Webhooks asymmetric variant, Discord) — SPEC lists it as out of scope; `std` has Ed25519. Effort: small. Fits §2: yes.
